article_title: Development of soft and hard skills of high-school students via Young Physicists' Tournament
citation: Sergej Faletič, Assen Kyuldjiev, Thomas Lindner, Dorottya Schnider, Éva Izsa, Mihály Hömöstrei, Péter Jenei, Boyka Aneva, Daniela D. Ivanova, Hynek Němec, František Kundracik, and Martin Plesch. (2022). Development of soft and hard skills of high-school students via Young Physicists' Tournament. https://www.iypt.org
title: Young Physicists' Tournament (YPT) format
description: YPT is a team competition for high-school students that closely mimics authentic physics research. Teams work for months on 17 open-ended annual problems and rotate in a graded debate through the roles of Reporter, Opponent and Reviewer before a jury of physicists. Problems are deliberately stated broadly, have no pre-defined correct answer, and require bibliographical research, experiment design, data analysis, theoretical modelling and English-language teamwork. The article surveys how this format is perceived to develop hard and soft skills.
requirements: Preparation times of 3 to 6 months for regional/national competitions and 8 or more months for IYPT
Teamwork in quinary teams with individual initiative
Good English skills since performances are in English
constraints: The demanding nature of the competition prevents massive participation of both students and teachers
target_learners: high-school students in the last two years of high school
examples: The problem Water Rise from the 26th IYPT, inspired by an observation of Philo from Byzantium, requires a properly designed experiment to resolve that the common oxygen-depletion explanation is wrong

title: YPT as authentic inquiry-based learning aligned with Authentic Science and ISLE
description: The article positions YPT within modern educational concepts, seeing it as closest to Authentic Science and the Investigative Science Learning Environment (ISLE), a well-proven learning system based on engaging students in a scientific reasoning process. YPT was born before these concepts became popular and developed without direct intent to apply specific didactic strategies. Its problems engage students in hypothetico-deductive reasoning: proposing explanations, building models, testing predictions against outcomes and explaining discrepancies. IYPT remains the only major international competition evaluating high-school students' inquiry-problem skills in physics.
requirements: Mastering the standard high-school curriculum is a prerequisite rather than the goal of the process
constraints: ISLE, as described, lacks the debate part; given the simple nature of its problems there is rarely disagreement among students or multiple solutions
examples: The YPT Toolkit reports two classroom implementations using simpler physics experiments ending with a report and peer opposition
